# Singletons reference

- [GameModeSingleton](#gamemodesingleton)
- [NavMarkerManager](#navmarkermanager)

## GameModeSingleton

`res://assets/scripts/singletons/GameMode.gd`, extends [`Node`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_node.html)

The shell of the game's rules: holds the game's modules. Autoload "GameMode".

"Game mode" is Unreal's name for this job. Here it holds optional modules and does almost nothing itself, so an empty one costs nothing, and each piece of a game's rules can be swapped or left out on its own.

The base's modules:
- [`PawnInitializer`](../game_mode/REFERENCE.md#pawninitializer): gives each pawn its default parts, from one list per game.
- [`PossessionCoordinator`](../game_mode/REFERENCE.md#possessioncoordinator): creates the PlayerController, and tracks who controls which pawn.
- [`AIActivationManager`](../game_mode/REFERENCE.md#aiactivationmanager): switches AI pawns off when no source keeps the ground under them loaded, and sets how often the rest run.
- [`SpawnManager`](../game_mode/REFERENCE.md#spawnmanager): puts pawns in at SpawnPoints, and brings players back after they die.
- [`ReplayRecorder`](../replay/REFERENCE.md#replayrecorder): records the game to a replay file once the game calls start_recording (replay spec).
- [`TeamRegistry`](../game_mode/REFERENCE.md#teamregistry): how many pawns are on each team.
- [`CrowdMover`](../movement/REFERENCE.md#crowdmover): moves AI pawns walking on the ground as one crowd.

How to use it:

```gdscript
GameMode.pawn_initializer         # a module, or null if this game doesn't have it, so check first
GameMode.possession_coordinator   # the same, and so on for each module above
GameMode.get_module(SomeScript)   # any module by its script
GameMode.add_module(node)         # a game's own modules, which extend GameModeModule
```

Which modules start with the game comes from the project setting "project_base/game_mode/modules", a list of script paths (with a ".release" override for release builds). With no setting, it starts the ones in `DEFAULT_MODULES`. An empty list starts none, and the game still runs.

What happens in odd cases (all checked in game_mode/tests/game_mode_selftest.gd):
- A path in the setting that doesn't load, or isn't a GameModeModule: it warns and carries on without that module.
- Adding a second module of the same type: it warns and keeps the first.

### Settings and properties

- `ai_activation_manager: AIActivationManager` = `null`: The module that switches AI pawns off, or null without one. Each module fills in its own line when it starts.
- `possession_coordinator: PossessionCoordinator` = `null`: Who controls which pawn, or null without one.
- `pawn_initializer: PawnInitializer` = `null`: Gives pawns their default parts, or null without one.
- `spawn_manager: SpawnManager` = `null`: Spawns pawns at spawn points and brings players back, or null without one.
- `replay_recorder: ReplayRecorder` = `null`: Records the game to replay files, or null without one (docs/replay/REPLAY_SPEC.md).
- `team_registry: TeamRegistry` = `null`: How many pawns are on each team, or null without one.
- `crowd_mover: CrowdMover` = `null`: Moves AI pawns walking on the ground as one crowd (pawn spec 8.22), or null without one.

### Signals

- `module_added(module: GameModeModule)`: Sent when a module has started.
- `module_removed(module: GameModeModule)`: Sent when a module has stopped, just before it's freed.

### Constants

- `MODULES_SETTING = "project_base/game_mode/modules"`: The project setting that lists the modules to start, as script paths.
- `DEFAULT_MODULES = Array[String](["res://assets/scripts/game_mode/PawnInitializer.gd", "res://assets/scripts/game_mode/PossessionCoordinator.gd", "res://assets/scripts/game_mode/AIActivationManager.gd", "res://assets/scripts/game_mode/SpawnManager.gd", "res://assets/scripts/replay/ReplayRecorder.gd", "res://assets/scripts/game_mode/TeamRegistry.gd", "res://assets/scripts/movement/CrowdMover.gd"])`: The modules started when the project setting isn't there, in this order.

### Functions

- `add_module(module: GameModeModule) -> void`: Starts a module. It stays until `remove_module()` or until the game ends.
- `remove_module(module: GameModeModule) -> void`: Stops a module and frees it. Anything using it should check again, because it's gone.
- `get_module(script: Script) -> GameModeModule`: The module made from this script, or null if there isn't one.
- `get_modules() -> GameModeModule[]`: Every module right now. Read it, don't change it.

## NavMarkerManager

`res://assets/scripts/singletons/NavMarkerManager.gd`, extends [`Node`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_node.html)

Holds every nav marker and answers searches for them. Autoload "NavMarkerManager".

It stores every nav marker, gives each a stable id, and answers searches like "the nearest point.cover within 20 m" (nav spec section 21.5). It needs no C++ library, so it works even where nav itself doesn't. It also keeps the list of marker modules, tells them when markers change, and reports types nothing handles. It doesn't find paths (NavServer does) or decide what a pawn does (AI does).

Written so its insides can move to C++ later without changing anything that calls it:
- Callers use only the public functions below, which take and return plain values.
- Searches return ids, not objects. `get_marker()` fetches the full data only when it's needed.
- What searches read sits in flat arrays ("rows"), not in one object per marker.
- A chunk registers its whole list in one call.
- Searches call no script code in their loops.
- Requests apply on the next tick, so nothing can rely on them being instant.
- Ids come from a hash written out here, because Godot's hash() could differ from a C++ version.

How it stores things: every marker is one row, meaning the same index in each array below. So _positions[7], _masks[7] and _ids[7] all describe one marker. A removed marker's row is reused later.

How search stays fast: the world is split into square cells, and a search only looks at nearby cells. Each cell keeps a linked list running through the rows. _cell_heads gives a cell's first row, and _next_in_cell gives the row after each one. That makes adding and removing a marker instant, and it keeps everything in flat arrays.

What happens in odd cases (all checked in navigation/tests/nav_marker_manager_selftest.gd):
- A duplicate id, an undeclared tag or a null marker: refused, with one warning for the whole list.
- An unknown id: harmless. get_marker gives null, and set_enabled warns and does nothing.
- Releasing a chunk that isn't registered: nothing happens.
- A search in an empty world, or with an infinite distance: finds what's there and always finishes.
- A search with an undeclared or empty tag: finds nothing, and doesn't add the tag.

Module rules are at the top of NavMarkerModule.gd, and checked in navigation/tests/nav_markers_selftest.gd.

The debug report: if markers exist of a type no module announced, it warns once per type, after registrations have gone quiet for `report_quiet_seconds`. It warns again only if a new unclaimed type appears, or a type loses its last module. Debug builds only. A level with no AI reports NavPoint, which is fine: it's one true line. Turn it off with the project setting `REPORT_SETTING`, for a game that leaves a type unhandled on purpose.

### Settings and properties

- `report_unhandled: bool` = `<unknown>`: Whether the automatic report runs. Starts from the project setting.
- `report_quiet_seconds: float` = `2.0`: How long registrations must stay quiet before the report runs, since a module may just not have arrived yet.

### Constants

- `REPORT_SETTING = "project_base/nav/report_unhandled_markers"`: The project setting that switches the debug report on or off (on by default).
- `CELL_SIZE = 32.0`: How wide each search cell is, in metres. Too small makes wide searches visit many cells, and too large makes each cell hold many markers.
- `NO_ROW = -1`: Means "no row", at the end of a linked list.
- `FNV_OFFSET = -3750763034362895579`
- `FNV_PRIME = 1099511628211`
- `Op.ADD = 0`
- `Op.REMOVE = 1`
- `Op.SET_ENABLED = 2`
- `Op.ADD_MODULE = 3`

### Functions

- `register_terrain(scene_path: String, settings: TerrainSettings) -> int`: A generator registers a copy of its settings, and gets the terrain id it uses for its chunks' markers. The id comes from the generator's scene path, so it matches on every machine, and across reloads, with nobody having to choose a number. Moving or renaming the node changes it. Registering again replaces the settings.
- `unregister_terrain(terrain: int) -> void`: Forgets a terrain's settings. Its chunks' markers leave through release_markers, not this.
- `get_terrain_settings(terrain: int) -> TerrainSettings`: A registered terrain's settings, or null if there's no such terrain.
- `chunk_of(terrain: int, position: Vector3) -> Vector2i`: Which chunk a position in the world is in, whether or not that chunk is loaded. Vector2i.ZERO for an unknown terrain.
- `request_markers(terrain: int, chunk: Vector2i, markers: NavMarker[]) -> int`: A chunk announces its markers. Returns how many were accepted; refused ones get one warning between them. A marker's id comes from its place in this list, so a generator must build the list the same way every time.
- `request_scene_marker(scene_path: String, marker: NavMarker) -> int`: A hand-placed marker asks to be registered. Returns its id, or 0 if it was refused. NavMarkerNode calls this with its scene path, so moving or renaming that node changes the id.
- `release_markers(terrain: int, chunk: Vector2i) -> void`: A chunk is unloading, so all its markers leave. Changes made to them are kept for when it comes back.
- `remove_scene_marker(id: int) -> void`: Removes one hand-placed marker. A chunk's markers leave through release_markers instead.
- `set_enabled(id: int, enabled: bool) -> void`: Switches a marker on or off. For a chunk's marker, the change is remembered through unloads, and only while it differs from how the marker started, so memory doesn't grow with the size of the world.
- `flush() -> void`: Applies every waiting request now, and tells modules. The tick does this by itself; tests and tools can call it directly.
- `add_module(module: NavMarkerModule) -> void`: A module entered the tree. It joins on the next tick, so its own _ready has run by the time it gets any calls.
- `remove_module(module: NavMarkerModule) -> void`: A module is leaving the tree. This happens straight away, not on the next tick, because the module may not exist by then. It gets a final _markers_removed so it can undo its work. The markers stay registered.
- `reset() -> void`: Forgets every marker and every kept change. For tests, and for leaving a level. Modules stay, and are told their markers have gone. Modules waiting to join still join on the next tick.
- `get_unhandled_types() -> Dictionary`: Types with markers that no module announced, as type name -> how many markers.
- `get_automatic_report_count() -> int`: How many automatic reports have been made since the last reset.
- `print_report() -> void`: Prints the same list on demand, in any build.
- `_type_is_claimed(type_index: int) -> bool`: True if a module that counts for the report handles this type.
- `find_nearest(tag: StringName, from: Vector3, max_distance: float) -> int`: The id of the nearest enabled marker matching the tag, within max_distance. 0 if there's none. Equal distances go to the lower id, so every machine picks the same marker.
- `find_in_radius(tag: StringName, from: Vector3, radius: float) -> PackedInt64Array`: The ids of every enabled marker matching the tag, within the radius. Sorted by id, so every machine gets the same order.
- `get_marker(id: int) -> NavMarker`: The full data for a marker, or null if there's no such id.
- `get_marker_position(id: int) -> Vector3`: Where a marker is. Vector3.ZERO if there's no such id.
- `is_marker_enabled(id: int) -> bool`: True if this marker is on. False for an unknown id.
- `get_marker_count() -> int`: How many markers are registered, applied or waiting for the next tick.
- `get_pending_count() -> int`: How many requests are waiting for the next tick.
- `get_kept_change_count() -> int`: How many marker changes are being remembered for chunks, loaded or not.
- `chunk_marker_id(terrain: int, chunk: Vector2i, index: int) -> int`: The same chunk and index give the same id on every machine, and after every reload.
- `scene_marker_id(scene_path: String) -> int`: A hand-placed marker's id, from its scene path: the same on every machine, and after every reload.
- `fnv_hash(bytes: PackedByteArray) -> int`: The FNV-1a hash of some bytes: for each byte, XOR it in and multiply by the prime. GDScript note: ints are 64 bits and wrap around when they overflow, which this relies on.
- `_why_refused(marker: NavMarker, id: int) -> String`: Why a marker can't be registered, or "" if it can.
- `_write_row(marker: NavMarker, id: int, from_chunk: bool) -> int`: Fills a row and returns its number. The marker isn't searchable until _link_row runs on the next tick.
- `_type_index_of(script: Script) -> int`: The number for a marker's type, adding the type the first time it's seen.
- `_find_modules_for(script: Script) -> Array`: Every joined module that handles this type or one of its parents.
- `_ids_handled_by(module: NavMarkerModule) -> PackedInt64Array`: The ids of every applied marker this module handles. It checks every row, so it's only for joining and leaving.
- `_tell_modules(rows: PackedInt32Array, what: int) -> void`: Gives each module one call, with the ids it handles out of these rows.
- `_link_row(row: int) -> void`: Puts a row at the front of its cell's linked list, which is what makes it searchable.
- `_unlink_row(row: int) -> void`: Takes a row out of its cell's linked list by joining its two neighbours to each other.
- `_cell_of(position: Vector3) -> Vector2i`: Which cell a position is in. Height doesn't matter, because the world is a flat plane with layers on it. GDScript note: floori rounds down, even for negatives, so -0.5 goes to cell -1 and not cell 0.
- `_search_bit(tag: StringName) -> int`: The tag's bit for searching, or 0 if nothing can match it. Never adds a tag.
- `_cells_in_ring(center: Vector2i, ring: int) -> Array`: The square ring of cells exactly this many cells away from the center.
- `_cells_within(from: Vector3, radius: float) -> Array`: Every cell a search of this radius has to look at, or just the occupied ones if that's fewer.

## NetworkSessionSingleton

`res://assets/scripts/singletons/NetworkSession.gd`, extends [`Node`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_node.html)

The multiplayer session (autoload "NetworkSession"): connects machines, spawns entities on all of them, and moves inputs and snapshots between them (netcode spec sections 4, 6, 10, 11).

Everything happens inside TickDriver's ticks. Nothing here is needed offline: with no session, entities play as single player.

The model is the standard one for competitive action games:
- The server is the authority. Clients send it inputs only, never positions or results.
- A client runs ahead of the server, so that its input for tick T arrives before the server runs T. Tick numbers mean the same thing everywhere, so "my prediction for tick T" can be compared with "the server's result for tick T".
- Your own pawn is predicted: it reacts at once, and when a snapshot says otherwise it's corrected (reconciliation).
- Everything else is drawn in the past between snapshots (entity interpolation).
- Attacks are checked by the server against what the shooter saw (lag compensation, see LagCompensation).

How to use it:

```gdscript
NetworkSession.register_type("pawn", preload("res://pawn.tscn"))  # same types in the same order on every machine
NetworkSession.world_root = $Entities
NetworkSession.host(port)   # or NetworkSession.join(address, port)
# On the server, whenever the game wants something to exist. A player joining spawns nothing by itself.
NetworkSession.spawn("pawn", peer_id, Vector3(0, 1, 0))
```

Snapshots carry each entity's changes since the last snapshot of it the client acknowledged (delta snapshots, netcode spec 11.4.1), cut into parts under ENet's packet size. Systems that aren't entities, such as terrain edits, send their own messages through world channels (server to clients) and client channels (client to server).

Time dilation (netcode spec section 4.2): the server reports how early each client's inputs have been arriving. A client cutting it too fine speeds up at once, going by the last half second. It only slows down again if the last 5 seconds have all been safe, so a rough connection keeps the lead it has shown it needs. Its lead settles on the smallest that gets inputs there in time, whatever the connection is doing. Only clients dilate. A client well behind where its clock says it should be, after a freeze say, jumps straight back instead of slowly catching up, because every tick behind is another input arriving too late.

Test tools: the fake bad network and switching features while running are in NetDebugModule, an optional child that fills `packet_filter`. Without one, this does none of that. See docs/TEST_AND_DEBUG_CODE.md.

One tick on a client: before_tick: world messages, then snapshots (which may roll back), then remote entities are moved; the tick's phases; after_tick: inputs and snapshot acknowledgements are sent.

One tick on the server: before_tick: received inputs are queued; the tick's phases; after_tick: snapshots are sent.

Rules, checked in tests/net_selftest.gd:
- A client with a different content hash is refused with a message saying so.
- Input for an entity the sender doesn't own, broken packets of any kind, and too many packets from one client are dropped.
- A snapshot older than the newest one seen is dropped. Input for a tick the server has already run is dropped, and the client gets corrected. The server repeats the last input when one is missing, and never rewinds for movement.
- A client that joins late gets everything that exists. Entities still owned by a client that leaves are removed. `player_leaving` fires first, so something can take back what it wants to keep. PossessionCoordinator does this for a possessed pawn, which stays in the world with no owner.

### Settings and properties

- `snapshot_rate: int` = `30`: Snapshots per second.
  
  A server's entities save their state only on snapshot ticks (NetworkEntity.refresh_input_saving), so changing this tells them.
- `interpolation_seconds: float` = `0.1`: How far in the past remote entities are drawn. Enough to always have two snapshots to blend between.
- `max_interpolation_seconds: float` = `0.2`: The most the adaptive version may draw in the past. Also limits how far back a client may claim to see.
- `lead_margin_ticks: int` = `3`: Extra ticks of lead beyond half the round trip, so input still arrives on time when the connection wobbles.
- `resync_threshold_ticks: int` = `4`: How far from its lead a client can drift before it jumps back, with dilation off.
- `resync_threshold_with_dilation_ticks: int` = `15`: How far ahead of its lead a client can drift before it jumps back, with dilation on. Dilation corrects gently, so this only covers things too big for that.
- `resync_behind_with_dilation_ticks: int` = `6`: With dilation on, being behind is treated more urgently than being ahead: a tick behind is an input lost.
- `dilation_margin_low_ticks: int` = `1`: Inputs should arrive at least this many ticks early. Below this in the last half second, the client speeds up.
- `dilation_margin_high_ticks: int` = `2`: If even the worst of the last 5 seconds is above this, the client is further ahead than it needs to be, and slows down.
- `dilation_gain: float` = `0.02`: How much to change speed per tick outside that range. Low enough not to overshoot on a late answer.
- `dilation_max_speedup: float` = `0.05`: The fastest a client will run, as a fraction above normal speed. A few percent isn't noticeable.
- `dilation_max_slowdown: float` = `0.03`: The slowest a client will run, as a fraction below normal speed.
- `prediction_enabled: bool` = `true`: Your own pawn reacts at once and gets corrected. Off: it waits for the server, so what you do shows up after your ping.
- `reconciliation_enabled: bool` = `true`: Your own pawn is corrected when the server disagrees. Off: it drifts, which shows what prediction alone would do.
- `interpolation_enabled: bool` = `true`: Remote entities are drawn in the past between snapshots. Off: they jump to each newest snapshot.
- `extrapolation_enabled: bool` = `true`: Remote entities move on from the newest snapshot if nothing newer has arrived. Off: they hold.
- `correction_smoothing_enabled: bool` = `true`: The visible model hides a correction's jump. Off: you see the jump.
- `follow_during_rollback: bool` = `false`: During a rollback, remote entities stand on server data rather than where they're drawn. See TickStateComponent.
- `time_dilation_enabled: bool` = `true`: A client's lead follows its connection. Off: it's set once, and jumps back when it drifts.
- `adaptive_interpolation_enabled: bool` = `true`: More jitter draws remote entities further in the past. Off: always interpolation_seconds.
- `delta_snapshots_enabled: bool` = `true`: Snapshots send each entity's changes since its baseline for that client: the newest snapshot whose part holding it the client acknowledged reading (per-part ACKs), instead of everything. Off: every entity in full, to compare.
- `rewind_cap_seconds: float` = `0.35`: How far back lag compensation may go. At 200 ms ping a shooter sees others about 350 ms behind its own tick (round trip, margin and interpolation), so this covers that and not much more. Past it, players have to lead their shots.
- `lag_compensation_enabled: bool` = `true`: Turns lag compensation off, to compare.
- `default_predicted: bool` = `false`: Project default for is_predicted on every entity. Entities can also turn it on for themselves.
- `input_redundancy: int` = `3`: How many inputs each input packet carries, the newest and some past ones, in case some are lost. Each extra one adds about 1.7 KB/s of upload. At 3, three packets in a row must be lost for an input to go missing.
- `missing_input_hold_ticks: int` = `3`: On the server, when a client's input goes missing, the last one repeats in full for this many ticks. Most losses are a tick or two. An entity can use its own number instead; Pawn has missing_input_hold_ticks for that.
- `missing_input_fade_ticks: int` = `6`: Then its direction fades to nothing over this many ticks, so a pawn whose player lost connection doesn't walk on forever. Pawn can override it with missing_input_fade_ticks.
- `use_native_encoding: bool` = `true`: Snapshots go through NetCodec in C++ when that library is here. Off, or with no library for this platform, they go through NetPackets instead. The bytes are the same, so machines of either kind can play together. Takes effect at host or join.
- `world_root: Node` = `null`: Where spawned entities go. Defaults to the current scene.
- `bind_address: String` = `"*"`: Which address the server listens on. "*" is all of them.
- `max_packets_per_second: int` = `2000`: Server: the most packets one client may send a second, so a broken or hostile client can't bury the server in work.
  
  Past this, or `max_bytes_per_second`, or with a packet over `max_packet_bytes`, its packets are dropped and counted in stats. 0 means no limit. A normal client sends about 60 packets and 6 KB a second for each pawn it controls, plus a few pings, so raise these for a game that gives one client over about 30 pawns.
- `max_bytes_per_second: int` = `262144`: Server: the most bytes one client may send a second. See `max_packets_per_second`.
- `max_packet_bytes: int` = `65536`: Server: the largest packet a client may send. See `max_packets_per_second`.
- `packet_filter: Object` = `null`: Something that can hold packets back on their way out and in, or null, which is normal. NetDebugModule fills it with its fake network. It has hold_outgoing(peer, bytes, reliable), hold_incoming(peer, bytes), release_due(now_usec) and clear().
- `stats: Dictionary` = `{...}`: Bytes and packets sent and received, and more, for diagnostics.
  
  On a server, snapshots_sent and snapshot_bytes (one per client per snapshot, and the bytes those carried), so their ratio is a client's average snapshot; on a client, snapshot_bytes_received with snapshots_received; snapshot_parts_received and deltas_without_baseline; and the biggest packet each way since the start.
- `render_tick: float` = `-1.0`: Client: which tick of the server's remote entities are being drawn at. -1 before the first snapshot.
- `server_load_percent: int` = `-1`: Client: how loaded the server's ticks are, as a percentage of their budget (TickDriver.load_average), from the newest snapshot. -1 before the first. The samples' status line shows it, for profiling different hardware.
- `server_load_step: int` = `-1`: Client: the server's load ladder step (TickDriver.load_step), from the newest snapshot. -1 before the first.

### Signals

- `hosted()`: Server: hosting has started.
- `joined()`: Client: connected, past the handshake, and ticking.
- `refused(reason: String)`: Client: couldn't join, and why.
- `disconnected()`: The connection ended (after `connection_ended` gives the reason).
- `player_connected(peer: int)`: Server: a client passed the handshake.
- `player_leaving(peer: int)`: Server: a client has gone, and what it owns hasn't been removed yet, so a listener can keep something by giving it a new owner.
- `player_left(peer: int)`: Server: a client has gone, and what it owned has been removed.
- `entity_spawned(entity: NetworkEntity)`: An entity was made on this machine, by spawn or a spawn packet.
- `entity_despawned(entity_id: int)`: An entity was removed on this machine.
- `entity_owner_changed(entity: NetworkEntity)`: An entity has a new owner, on every machine.
- `connection_ended(peer: int, reason: String, details: Dictionary)`: A connection ended, and why, for diagnostics.
  
  On a client, peer is 1 (the server), sent just before `disconnected`. On a server, once for each client that goes, and once with peer 0 when the server itself stops. reason is plain text. details has "seconds_connected", "seconds_since_heard" (since the last packet from that peer), and "rtt_ms" and "loss_percent" (the connection's last round trip and packet loss as ENet measured them, -1 if never measured).

### Constants

- `Mode.OFFLINE = 0`
- `Mode.SERVER = 1`
- `Mode.CLIENT = 2`
- `SERVER_FEATURES = Array[String](["lag_compensation_enabled", "default_predicted"])`: The settings the server decides for everyone, so snapshots say what they are.
- `NO_MARGIN = 32767`: What snapshots say when a client has sent no input lately.
- `MARGIN_SHORT_WINDOW = 30`: How many recent input packets count for the quick check that speeds up: half a second at 60 a second.
- `MARGIN_LONG_WINDOW = 300`: How many recent input packets count for the slow check that slows down: 5 seconds at 60 a second.
- `COUNTING_STATS = Array[String](["bytes_sent", "bytes_received", "snapshots_encoded", "snapshots_sent", "snapshot_bytes", "snapshots_received", "snapshot_bytes_received", "corrections", "resyncs", "interpolation_underruns"])`: The stats that only ever count up, which diagnostics turns into rates and averages per frame. Renaming one here renames it there, since diagnostics names none of them itself.
- `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT = 5.0`: Seconds a new connection has to pass the handshake before the server drops it.
- `SAMPLES_BEFORE_TICKING = 6`: Pongs a client waits for before it sets its clock and starts ticking.
- `PING_INTERVAL_STARTING = 0.05`: Seconds between a client's pings while it's setting its clock.
- `PING_INTERVAL = 0.25`: Seconds between a client's pings once its clock is set.
- `BUILD_ID_SETTING = "project_base/network/build_id"`: The project setting that names a build. See `content_hash()`.
- `HASHED_FILE_TYPES = PackedStringArray("gd", "gdc", "tscn", "scn", "tres", "res")`: The file types `content_hash()` reads when no build id is set.
- `MAX_INBOX_PER_PEER = 128`: Most packets the server keeps from one client between ticks, so one client can't crowd out others. A client sends one per pawn per tick, and they pile up while the server is frozen, so this has room for 4 pawns through a freeze of half a second. A client doesn't cap what its server sends (see handle_packet).
- `MAX_INPUTS_PER_PACKET = 16`: Most inputs one packet may carry. Fixed, because input_redundancy is a setting each machine has its own copy of.
- `SNAPSHOT_PART_BYTES = 1100`: Snapshots are split into parts of at most this many bytes of entities, each its own packet, so none goes over ENet's packet size (1392 bytes) and the loss of one piece doesn't lose the whole snapshot.
- `DELTA_ID_BIT = 2147483648`: An entity's id with this bit set means its state list is a delta: [ticks back to the baseline, the change masks, the changed values]. Ids never get this high.
- `DELTA_MASK_BITS = 30`: How many state entries each change mask covers. 30 keeps a mask an int of at most 5 bytes, and 1 or 2 when only the first few entries changed.
- `DELTA_MAX_BASELINE_AGE = 48`: The oldest baseline a delta may use, in ticks. Both sides keep 64 ticks, so this leaves room. A client that hasn't acknowledged anything this recent gets everything in full.
- `BASELINE_RING = 64`: How many ticks of received state a client keeps per entity, for decoding deltas.
- `NET_MONITORS_SCRIPT = "res://assets/scripts/netcode/debug/NetMonitors.gd"`: The debugger graphs' script, loaded only if it's there (see _ready).
- `MAX_ACK_ENTRIES = 8`: The most ticks one ACK packet may name. A client sends at most this many, and the server refuses a packet claiming more, so one packet can't make it walk through a long made-up list.
- `LINK_CHECK_INTERVAL_USEC = 500000`: How often each connection's round trip and packet loss are read from ENet, in microseconds.

### Functions

- `_new_peer(welcomed: bool) -> NetworkSessionSingleton.PeerRecord`: A new client's record. Tests make theirs with this too.
- `register_type(type_name: String, scene: PackedScene) -> void`: Adds a type of entity that can be spawned. Every machine must add the same ones.
- `get_type_scene(type_name: String) -> PackedScene`: The scene registered for this type name, or null. SpawnManager reads a type's team from it.
- `host(port: int, max_clients: int = 32) -> int`: Starts a server. Returns OK or an error.
- `join(address: String, port: int) -> int`: Connects to a server. joined or refused follows later. Returns OK or an error.
- `leave() -> void`: Ends the session and removes everything it spawned. Safe to call at any time.
- `get_mode() -> int`: Whether this machine is offline, a server or a client.
- `is_server() -> bool`: True on a server (a host).
- `get_match_options() -> PackedStringArray`: The settings a start menu may offer before a match (MatchOptionsPanel.add_from_autoloads): the snapshots. The host's decide for everyone.
- `get_newest_snapshot_tick() -> int`: Client: the tick of the newest snapshot that has arrived, -1 before any. How fast it climbs is how fast the server is really ticking, which the samples' status line shows.
- `is_client() -> bool`: True on a client, from join until it leaves.
- `get_local_peer() -> int`: This machine's peer id. Offline, and on the server, it's 1.
- `is_connected_to_session() -> bool`: True while a real connection is up (not offline, and connected).
- `get_rtt_ms() -> float`: Client: the measured round trip in milliseconds.
- `get_lead_ticks() -> float`: Client: how many ticks ahead of the server it's actually running.
- `get_view_ticks_behind() -> float`: Client: how many ticks behind its own tick remote entities are drawn. Attacks send this, for lag compensation.
- `get_tick_factor() -> float`: Client: how fast its ticks are running compared to normal.
- `get_input_margin() -> int`: Client: the worst the server has lately seen its inputs arrive, in ticks early. Negative is late. NO_MARGIN if unknown.
- `get_missed_inputs() -> int`: Client: how many of its inputs the server has had to do without.
- `limit_view_ticks_behind(peer: int, claimed: float, tick: int) -> float`: How many ticks behind its own tick a client can believably be drawing others, for lag compensation. It can't be drawing anything newer than the snapshot it last acknowledged, and it can't be further behind that than the interpolation limit. Acknowledgements only ever move forward, and one older than the rewind cap gets no rewind. A client that deliberately acknowledges late still gets through, but that looks exactly like really having high ping, so this can't stop it entirely. Offline, the host's own pawn and AI aren't limited.
- `content_hash() -> int`: A number that's the same on two machines only if they run the same content. The handshake refuses a client whose number differs.
  
  It covers the packet format, the tag sets (abilities, nav) and the named input actions, the engine build, every physics setting, the game's own files, and every registered entity type's TickStateComponent schema. Not the tick rate: the server chooses that for the match and hands it over in WELCOME, after this is checked.
  
  Set the project setting `BUILD_ID_SETTING` to give a build a name instead of reading its files. That's the normal way for a release: stamp the build number when exporting, and only builds with the same number play together. Also use it if the same project on different operating systems refuses itself, since line endings can differ.
- `_add_file_hashes(folder: String, parts: PackedStringArray) -> void`: The name and contents of every script, scene and resource in this folder and below. Folders starting with a dot are skipped: that's Godot's cache, and git's. An exported game has the same kinds of files, in their packed forms.
- `spawn(type_name: String, owner_peer: int, at: Variant) -> Node`: Server or offline: makes an entity on this machine and on every client. owner_peer sends its input; 0 is the server itself.
- `despawn(entity_id: int) -> void`: Server or offline: removes an entity everywhere.
- `set_entity_owner(entity_id: int, new_owner: int) -> void`: Server or offline: gives an entity to another player, or to nobody with 0. Every client hears about it. From then on, its input comes from the new owner, and the new owner's machine predicts it.
- `get_entity(entity_id: int) -> NetworkEntity`: The entity with this id, or null.
- `get_entities() -> NetworkEntity[]`: Every live entity, in id order. The same list each time, rebuilt only when entities come and go, because several per-tick paths use it. Read it, don't change it.
- `refresh_entities() -> void`: A switch changed: every entity works out its role again. NetDebugModule calls it after a feature switch, and a client after the server's features arrive.
- `send_now(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray, reliable: bool) -> void`: Sends bytes straight away, past `packet_filter`. NetDebugModule hands it to its fake network to send what it held back.
- `_on_packet(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> void`: Everything arriving comes through here. Connection packets act at once. Inputs and snapshots wait for the next tick, so they're applied at a fixed point in the tick's order.
- `_within_limits(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> bool`: Server: may this client send this packet now? Until it has passed the handshake, it may only send the packet that does that. Every packet counts against the per-second limits, pings included.
- `handle_packet(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray, _reliable: bool) -> void`: Acts on one arrived packet, after `packet_filter`. NetDebugModule hands it to its fake network to deliver what it held back.
- `_drop_silent_peers() -> void`: A client that connected but never finished the handshake, or was refused and stayed.
- `_new_link() -> Dictionary`: A new connection's numbers.
- `_check_links(now: int) -> void`: Every LINK_CHECK_INTERVAL_USEC, each connection's round trip and packet loss as ENet measures them, kept because ENet can't be asked once a connection has gone. GDScript note: "as" gives null when the peer isn't an ENetMultiplayerPeer (a test's own kind of peer), so those are skipped.
- `get_link_stats() -> Dictionary`: Each connection's last known numbers, peer -> {"seconds_connected", "seconds_since_heard", "rtt_ms", "loss_percent"}. On a client the one connection is peer 1, the server. Diagnostics shows these in its summaries.
- `_jump_back_if_drifted() -> void`: Client: jumps the tick back to its target if it has drifted too far. Checked every frame rather than when a ping returns, so a client that froze is back on time at once. The clock goes by the fastest recent ping, so a lag spike doesn't look like falling behind.
- `register_world_channel(channel: String, receive: Callable, catch_up: Callable = Callable()) -> void`: Sets up a channel. receive(bytes) runs on clients. catch_up() runs on the server when a client joins, and returns the bytes to send it, or empty for nothing.
- `unregister_world_channel(channel: String) -> void`: Removes a channel set up with `register_world_channel()`.
- `send_world_message(channel: String, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> void`: Server: sends bytes to every client on a channel. Does nothing anywhere else.
- `_on_world_message(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> void`: Only a server sends these, so anyone else sending one is misbehaving.
- `register_client_channel(channel: String, receive: Callable) -> void`: Sets up a channel. receive(peer, bytes) runs on the server.
- `unregister_client_channel(channel: String) -> void`: Removes a channel set up with `register_client_channel()`.
- `send_to_server(channel: String, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> void`: Client: sends bytes to the server on a channel. Does nothing anywhere else.
- `_profile_part(part: StringName, mark: int) -> int`: Adds the time since mark to one network part of a tick, in the driver's timing record. Returns now, the next part's mark.
- `get_snapshot_interval() -> int`: Ticks between snapshots: a server sends one when the tick is a multiple of this. 1 without a tick driver.
- `_send_inputs(tick: int) -> void`: Client: sends this tick's input for each entity it controls, plus a few past ones in case some were lost.
- `_send_part_acks() -> void`: Client: says which snapshot parts it has read since the last time, one ACK packet a tick at most: [ACK, how many ticks (up to 8, newest first), then for each: the tick (u32), its part count (u8), and a bit per part (1 = read, every entity in it)]. Sent unreliably: a lost ACK only means the server keeps using older baselines for those entities, and the next snapshot's parts are acknowledged as usual.
- `_note_part_read(tick: int, part: int, part_count: int) -> void`: Client: notes that it read a part of a snapshot, every entity in it, for the next ACK.
- `_on_ack(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> void`: Server: a client says which parts of which snapshots it read. Every entity that was in a part it read now has that tick as its baseline for this client (if newer than the one it had), so the next snapshot can send it as changes since then. Parts of a snapshot the server no longer remembers sending, and ticks that haven't happened, are ignored. It also counts for lag compensation, like the field in input packets: it only moves forward.
- `_on_input(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray, tick: int) -> void`: Server: stores a client's inputs for the ticks they belong to. Only the owner may send them, and they're cleaned first.
- `_margins_to_report(info: NetworkSessionSingleton.PeerRecord, tick: int) -> PackedInt32Array`: Server: the two timing reports for a client's next snapshot, [the worst margin over the last half second, over the last 5]. NO_MARGIN for either that isn't known. A client whose newest input is older than the short window (it stopped sending: spectating, or its pawn died) gets NO_MARGIN for both, and its old margins are dropped, so it doesn't keep speeding up or slowing down on them.
- `_note_input_timing(peer: int, newest: int, acknowledged: int, tick: int) -> void`: Server: how early this input packet arrived, for time dilation. Only packets bringing something new count: a duplicate, or one overtaken on the way, isn't late input, because the server already has what it carries. What a client acknowledges only moves forward, and a client can't have seen the future.
- `_make_codec(expected_protocol: int) -> Object`: NetCodec if it's usable. Falls back to NetPackets if the library is missing, or was built for another packet format and would need rebuilding. Asking for it by name means this script still runs on a platform without the library.
- `is_using_native_encoding() -> bool`: True if snapshots are going through C++ right now.
- `_is_in_snapshot(entity: NetworkEntity, tick: int) -> bool`: Whether an entity goes in this tick's snapshot. It does if it recorded this tick, even with no state list at all: an entity whose only state is save_state() data, or that has only sync properties, records its ticks too. A paused entity records nothing, so it's left out.
- `_send_snapshots(tick: int) -> void`: Server: sends the world to every client, with a note for each on how its input is arriving, for time dilation.
- `_snapshot_entry(entity: NetworkEntity, tick: int, id: int, state_values: Array, state_encodings: Array) -> Array`: One entity's lists for the codec, as write_world takes them, with the given id and state list.
- `_delta_entity_bytes(entity: NetworkEntity, tick: int, baseline: int) -> PackedByteArray`: An entity encoded as its changes since baseline, or empty if it has to go in full (no state list, nothing saved for the baseline tick, or a list too long for one).
  
  The state list becomes [tick - baseline, mask, mask, ..., the changed values], and the id gets DELTA_ID_BIT. Each mask covers DELTA_MASK_BITS entries in order, a bit set for each that changed. An entity that changed nothing still sends its id, the ticks back and its empty masks.
- `delta_state_lists(now: Array, then: Array, encodings: Array, ticks_back: int) -> Array` *(static)*: The change check for a delta: [values, encodings] to send, [ticks_back, mask, mask, ..., each changed value].
  
  now and then are an entity's state values at this tick and at its baseline, ticks_back the ticks between them. Empty if the lists differ in length or the result is too long for one list. A value is unchanged when its type and value are both the same. The C++ one (NetCodec.delta_state) gives the same lists, and tests/net_codec_selftest compares them.
  
  GDScript note: static, so it can be called on the class without a session (NetworkSessionSingleton.delta_state_lists(...)).
- `_cut_into_parts(chunks: PackedByteArray[], ids: PackedInt32Array) -> NetworkSessionSingleton.SnapshotPart[]`: Groups encoded entities into parts of at most SNAPSHOT_PART_BYTES each (one bigger than that goes alone), with the entity id of each chunk (ids, in the same order). Always at least one part, so a snapshot with no entities still arrives. At most 255 parts.
- `_apply_server_features(mask: int) -> void`: Client: the features the server decides are whatever it says. default_predicted changes roles here, so this matters in a real game too.
- `_on_snapshot(peer: int, bytes: PackedByteArray) -> void`: Client: remote entities store what the snapshot says. Predicted ones keep it aside for _reconcile, newest only.
- `_rebuild_from_delta(entity: NetworkEntity, tick: int, delta: Array) -> Variant`: Client: the full state list from a delta ([ticks back, masks..., changed values]) and what this client kept for that entity at the baseline tick. Null if the baseline isn't here or the delta doesn't fit.
- `_keep_baseline(entity_id: int, tick: int, values: Array) -> void`: Client: keeps what the server sent for an entity on a tick, to decode later deltas against.
- `_reconcile() -> void`: Client: compares predictions with the newest snapshot, and if any are wrong, corrects them and resimulates from there.
- `_move_remote_entities() -> void`: Client: moves the drawing clock on one tick, keeping it a fixed distance behind the newest snapshot, then places every remote entity. It runs slightly fast or slow to catch up rather than jumping, so motion stays smooth.
- `_interpolation_ticks() -> float`: How far behind the newest snapshot to draw. With jitter, snapshots arrive unevenly, so it draws further back to keep having two to blend between.
- `_note_snapshot_timing(tick: int) -> void`: How unevenly snapshots are arriving, as a slow average of how far each is from when it was expected.
- `_update_dilation(margin: int, margin_long: int) -> void`: Client: the server said how early our inputs have been arriving, at worst, over the last half second and the last 5. Too close over the short one: speed up, more the further out it is. Plenty to spare over the whole of the long one: slow down. Otherwise, normal speed. The difference is deliberate: being late costs inputs, and being early only costs a little.
- `set_tick_factor(factor: float) -> void`: Client: sets how fast its ticks run compared to normal (time dilation), and notes the extremes in stats. NetDebugModule calls it too, to go back to normal speed.

## TickDriverSingleton

`res://assets/scripts/singletons/TickDriver.gd`, extends [`Node`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_node.html)

The tick driver: runs all gameplay in numbered, fixed-length ticks, online and offline. Autoload "TickDriver".

Every machine runs it. All gameplay simulation runs inside its ticks, in a fixed phase order, instead of in each node's own _process/_physics_process. The abilities, the AI and the netcode all run on it. Design: netcode spec section 3, and scaling spec section 7 for the tick rate.

How an entity takes part:

```gdscript
TickDriver.register(self)    # a Pawn, TickStateComponent or NetworkEntity does this itself in _enter_tree
TickDriver.unregister(self)  # or just get freed; freed participants are dropped automatically
```

and implements any of these (all optional; a participant only gets the calls it has):

```gdscript
func _tick_input(dt: float, tick: int) -> void      # phase 1: controllers write this tick's input command
func _tick_capture_input(tick: int) -> void         # phase 2: save the input for replay (usually TickStateComponent)
func _tick_simulate(dt: float, tick: int) -> void   # phase 3: abilities, movement, move_and_slide
func _tick_record(tick: int) -> void                # phase 4: predicted parts save their state
```

dt is **always** the fixed tick length, never the frame's delta.

Gotcha: if a participant also defines _physics_process (as a fallback when there's no driver, say), turn it off with set_physics_process(false) in _ready, not _enter_tree. Godot switches it on at ready, and the object would then tick twice. Example: assets/scripts/samples/TickSamplePawn.gd.

One tick runs: `before_tick`, every _tick_input, every _tick_capture_input, every _tick_simulate, `after_simulate`, every _tick_record, `after_tick`. A frame runs as many ticks as the elapsed time covers (usually exactly one), wrapped in `before_tick_loop` and `after_tick_loop`.

Rules and corner cases (all checked in tests/tick_driver_selftest.gd):
- Order within a phase: lower `order` first (register's second argument, default 0); equal order keeps registration order. Every machine registers a level's pawns in the same order, so they run in the same order.
- Registering twice changes nothing (the first registration stands). Unregistering an unknown object does nothing.
- Registering during a tick takes effect from the next tick. Unregistering during a tick stops its calls at once (a pawn despawned mid-tick isn't simulated or recorded afterwards).
- A freed participant is skipped and dropped, never called.
- Catch-up spiral: at most `max_ticks_per_frame` ticks per frame. Time beyond that is dropped (the game slows down instead of freezing) and counted in `dropped_ticks`.
- `tick_factor` scales how fast ticks happen (time dilation): the netcode nudges it on clients, and it's 1.0 offline and on the server.
- A frame running more than one tick (dilation, catching up, or a tick_rate above the physics rate) calls each participant's optional _sync_collision() between its ticks, so bodies collide with each other's latest positions, as they would with one tick per frame. Frames with one tick pay nothing. `step()` is for tests, and doesn't do this. Only entities with a TickStateComponent get this; a body moved by anything else stays out of date until the step.
- `active` = false pauses ticking; nothing builds up while paused.
- Runs in _physics_process, so physics queries are safe during ticks. The default tick_rate is the project's physics rate, and the autoload sets physics to the tick rate anyway (`physics_follows_tick_rate`), so it's one tick per physics frame.
- move_and_slide scales velocity by Godot's physics delta, not by the tick. If tick_rate differs from the physics rate, a motor multiplies velocity by `get_physics_factor()` before move_and_slide and divides after.

**The load ladder** (pawn spec 8.21, the owner's call). Each tick's cost is measured against its budget (the tick's length). While ticks use more than `raise_above` of it for `raise_after_ticks`, `load_step` doubles (1, 2, 4). It halves again after `lower_after_ticks` ticks in a row under `lower_below`, or in a row where the load it predicts for the lower step, from what stepping up saved, fits under raise_above less `step_down_headroom` (see _lower_step_fits). The AIActivationManager makes every AI pawn run at most every load_step-th tick, so an overloaded game sheds AI work, the bulk of a tick, instead of falling behind: the whole game's AI at 30 (or 15) ticks a second, with every timer still lasting as long (Pawn.ticks_elapsed). Players' pawns always run every tick. Tick numbers don't change, so nothing in the netcode does either. `load_step_override` forces a step; `load_ladder_enabled` off keeps it at 1.

**Rollback** (netcode spec section 3.5). `rollback()` puts predicted participants back to how they ended from_tick, then replays every later tick up to the last finished one. A participant is predicted if it has _rollback_load(tick) -> bool, _rollback_input(tick), _rollback_simulate(dt, tick) and _tick_record(tick). TickStateComponent provides all four, so entities normally just add that node. Rules, also tested:
- While replaying: `is_resimulating()` is true (cosmetic effects must check it), `tick` reads as the tick being replayed, and the `tick_rng()` rolls repeat exactly. Input phases don't run; saved inputs are restored instead.
- Everything not predicted stays where it is during the replay, the standard accepted inaccuracy. The exception is an entity in FOLLOW_SERVER mode with follows_during_rollback on: it stands on server data, extrapolates past it on its velocity, then returns to where it was.
- Each replaying participant's optional _rollback_finished() runs once the replay is over, before `after_rollback`.
- Loading happens in stages: resimulated participants load first. If none could, nothing happens and it returns false, because a replay would have nothing to do. Following ones then join if they want to and are near one of those (wants_to_join_rollback). Then collision positions sync, then each one's optional _rollback_after_load(tick) runs, so a floor check there sees everyone else in place. is_resimulating() is true through all of this and the finish step.
- When two or more participants replay, each one's optional _sync_collision() runs after loading and after each replayed tick, so physics bodies collide with each other's replayed positions rather than their final ones.
- Allowed between ticks or from before_tick (where the netcode applies snapshots). During the phases, or during another replay, it warns and returns false.
- With physics bodies, call it during the physics frame (before_tick is). Outside it, move_and_slide uses the rendered frame's delta instead, so replayed movement would be the wrong length.
- A participant that no longer has from_tick keeps its current state and sits the replay out.
- Returns false if nothing could be loaded or from_tick is in the future. No side effects then.

### Settings and properties

- `tick_rate: int` = `0`: Ticks per second. 0 (the default): the project setting, or else the project's physics rate. Chosen before a match starts and not changed during it (scaling spec section 7): clients take the server's in the handshake, before anything spawns. A dedicated server can choose it at start-up with `-- --tick-rate=30`. Settings counted in ticks are written for 60 a second and converted with `ticks_at_rate()`.
- `max_ticks_per_frame: int` = `3`: Most ticks one frame may run, so a slow frame can't cause ever more ticks (a catch-up spiral). The rest of the time is dropped: an overloaded game slows down instead of freezing.
  
  The autoload sets Godot's own limit on physics steps a frame (Engine.max_physics_steps_per_frame) to the same number. Each physics step runs one tick, so Godot's limit is the one that really counts.
- `physics_follows_tick_rate: bool` = `true`: On, the autoload sets Godot's physics rate to the tick rate whenever the rate is chosen, so there's one tick per physics step and the physics engine doesn't step twice for every tick at 30. Pawns are drawn between ticks anyway (Visual's smoothing). Turn it off to keep physics at the project's rate with ticks at another.
- `active: bool` = `true`: False pauses ticking.
- `tick: int` = `0`: Current tick number: the last tick that ran. Starts at 0 before any tick. Change it only with `set_tick()`.
- `tick_factor: float` = `1.0`: Time dilation multiplier: how fast ticks happen. 1.0 offline and on the server; on a client the netcode nudges it to keep its clock right (NetClock).
- `dropped_ticks: int` = `0`: Ticks skipped by the max_ticks_per_frame limit, and time Godot dropped beyond its own limit, for diagnostics.
- `load_ladder_enabled: bool` = `true`: On, load_step follows how loaded the ticks are. Off, it stays at 1 (unless load_step_override says otherwise).
- `max_load_step: int` = `4`: The highest load_step the ladder goes to: 1, 2 or 4.
- `load_step_override: int` = `0`: 0 (the default): automatic. 1, 2 or 4: forced, for testing a level or a game that wants one.
- `raise_above: float` = `0.85`: The share of a tick's budget above which the ladder steps up, after raise_after_ticks in a row.
- `raise_after_ticks: int` = `30`: How many ticks in a row over raise_above before it steps up, at 60 a second. 30: half a second.
- `lower_below: float` = `0.4`: The share of a tick's budget below which the ladder always steps down, after lower_after_ticks in a row. It also steps down when it predicts the lower step fits (`step_down_headroom`): much of a tick doesn't shrink with the AI's step (recording, the player's pawn, the replay), so a game at step 4 can sit at about half its budget, never under this line.
- `step_down_headroom: float` = `0.15`: The ladder also steps down when the load it predicts for the lower step is under raise_above minus this, after lower_after_ticks in a row. The prediction is the load now plus what stepping up saved when it last did (measured: the load just before the step up, less the load once it had settled). With no measurement yet, it assumes the load doubles.
- `saving_measured_after_ticks: int` = `30`: How long after a step up the load is measured again to work out what it saved, in ticks at 60 a second. About three times what the average takes to settle.
- `smallest_believable_saving: float` = `0.05`: A measured saving under this share of the budget is treated as not measured (the load probably rose for another reason while measuring, such as a fight starting), so stepping down assumes the load doubles instead of that it barely changes, which would bounce the ladder up and down.
- `lower_after_ticks: int` = `180`: How many ticks in a row under lower_below (or with the lower step predicted to fit) before it steps down, at 60 a second. 180: three seconds.
- `load_step: int` = `1`: The most every AI pawn may run, as a step: 1 every tick, 2 every 2nd, 4 every 4th. Read it; set load_step_override to force it.
- `load_average: float` = `0.0`: How much of its budget a tick has used lately, smoothed over about ten ticks: 1.0 is the whole tick's length.
- `profile_enabled: bool` = `false`: On, each tick phase adds up its time in microseconds into `profile`, for finding what's slow. Off, it costs a few checks of this flag per tick.
- `profile: Dictionary` = `{}`: Each phase's time in microseconds, and the counts in PROFILE_COUNTS, while profile_enabled is on. Emptied by `reset_profile()`.

### Signals

- `before_tick_loop()`: Sent once a frame, before the frame's first tick. Not sent in a frame with no tick due.
- `before_tick(dt: float, tick: int)`: Sent at the start of each tick, before any phase. The netcode applies snapshots here, and may roll back from it.
- `after_tick(dt: float, tick: int)`: Sent at the end of each tick, after every phase. A rollback from here counts this tick as finished.
- `after_simulate(dt: float, tick: int)`: Sent after every participant has simulated and before anything is recorded (pawn spec 15.1). Effects one entity queued for another during simulate, such as hits, are delivered here, so they never depend on which simulated first. Not sent during a rollback's replay.
- `after_tick_loop()`: Sent once a frame, after the frame's last tick. Delays counted in ticks (SpawnManager's, say) run here, between ticks.
- `after_rollback(from_tick: int, to_tick: int)`: Sent when a rollback's replay is over: it went back to from_tick and replayed up to to_tick.
- `rollback_state_loaded(from_tick: int)`: State is back to from_tick, and the replay is about to run. A correction can put a pawn somewhere new here, and anything that has to be ready before it moves, such as the ground, gets its chance now.
- `load_step_changed(step: int)`: Sent when `load_step` changes (the load ladder; see the class description).

### Constants

- `TICK_RATE_SETTING = "project_base/network/tick_rate"`: The project setting for the tick rate. 0 or missing: the project's physics rate.
- `REFERENCE_RATE = 60`: Settings counted in ticks are written for 60 ticks a second, whatever rate a game runs at, so designers tune in the same numbers everywhere. ticks_at_rate() turns one into ticks at the rate this match runs at.
- `PROFILE_COUNTS = Array[String](["ticks", "rollbacks", "rollback_ticks"])`: The entries of `profile` that count things. The rest are times in microseconds.

### Functions

- `register(participant: Object, order: int = 0) -> void`: Adds a participant. `order`: lower runs first within each phase.
- `unregister(participant: Object) -> void`: Removes a participant. During a tick, its calls stop at once.
- `is_registered(participant: Object) -> bool`: True if this participant is registered.
- `get_participant_count() -> int`: How many participants are registered.
- `advance(elapsed: float) -> void`: Feeds elapsed time in and runs the ticks it covers. Called every physics frame while active; tests call it directly.
- `step() -> void`: Runs exactly one tick now, whatever the time. For tests and tools.
- `get_tick_rate() -> int`: Ticks per second this match runs at.
- `ticks_at_rate(reference_ticks: int) -> int`: A setting counted in ticks at the reference rate (60 a second), as ticks at this match's rate, so it lasts the same time: round(ticks × rate ÷ 60), and at least 1 where the setting is above 0. 0 and negative settings (which usually mean "off" or "use the default") come back as they are. At 60 it changes nothing. An 8-tick wind-up is 8 ticks at 60 and 4 at 30: 0.13 s either way. A setting that doesn't divide evenly is up to half a tick off.
- `per_tick_at_rate(reference_amount: float) -> float`: An amount added each tick at the reference rate (sight's fill_rate, say), as the amount each tick at this match's rate adds, so the total over a second is the same: amount × 60 ÷ rate.
- `get_tick_dt() -> float`: Length of one tick in seconds.
- `get_physics_factor() -> float`: Multiply velocity by this before move_and_slide (and divide after) so a tick moves the pawn velocity * tick_dt even when tick_rate isn't the physics rate. 1.0 when they match.
- `get_interpolation_fraction() -> float`: How far between the last tick and the next one we are, 0..1. For smoothing visuals per rendered frame.
- `seconds_to_ticks(seconds: float) -> int`: Seconds (as designers type them) to whole ticks. Any time above zero is at least one tick, so a short buffer window or cooldown never silently becomes zero.
- `ticks_to_seconds(ticks: int) -> float`: Ticks to seconds at this match's rate.
- `set_tick(new_tick: int) -> void`: Jumps to a tick number. For a client setting its clock from the server's; use nothing else to change tick. Not allowed during a tick. Saved history stays valid, because each slot remembers which tick it holds.
- `is_resimulating() -> bool`: True while a rollback is replaying ticks. Cosmetic effects (sounds, particles) should not fire then.
- `is_in_tick() -> bool`: True while a tick runs, from before_tick to after_tick. A request aimed at another pawn's AI made then is queued and applied at that pawn's next AI step (pawn spec 15.1), so it never depends on which pawn went first.
- `is_in_simulate() -> bool`: True while a tick's simulate phase runs (not a rollback's replay). An effect aimed at another entity during it is queued and delivered from after_simulate (pawn spec 15.1).
- `tick_rng(key: int, salt: int = 0) -> RandomNumberGenerator`: Repeatable randomness for gameplay, instead of randf(). The rolls depend only on key, tick and salt, so a replay of the same tick gets the same results and there's no generator state to save. Use it right away; the same object is returned every call. key is usually an entity id; salt separates rolls within a tick.
- `rollback(from_tick: int) -> bool`: Puts predicted participants back to how they ended from_tick and replays up to the last finished tick. See the rules in the class description. Returns true if a replay happened.
- `_load_for_rollback(from_tick: int) -> Array`: Loads resimulated participants, then the following ones near them. Far-away following entities are skipped, which is what keeps a large swarm affordable. Empty if no resimulated participant could load.
- `_sync_collision_world() -> void`: Brings every body's collision up to date between two ticks of one frame. One body alone never collides with itself, so this only does anything for two or more.
- `reset_profile() -> void`: Empties the timing record. See profile_enabled.
- `is_authority() -> bool`: True where gameplay outcomes are decided. Offline: always. Online: the server.
- `get_match_options() -> PackedStringArray`: The settings a start menu may offer before a match (MatchOptionsPanel.add_from_autoloads): the load ladder.
- `_lower_step_fits() -> bool`: True if the next step down looks safe now: the load is under lower_below, or the load predicted for the lower step (the load now plus what this step saved, or twice the load if that isn't known) is under raise_above less step_down_headroom.
- `_profile_phase(phase: StringName, mark: int) -> int`: Adds the time since mark to this phase, and returns the new mark.
- `_rebuild_phases() -> void`: Sorts participants and splits them by the phase methods they have. Only runs when the registry changed, never per tick. Also drops freed participants.
